frozen_question: Are Plutarch's nineteenth-day proclamation that Osiris is found and the Papyrus Jumilhac nineteenth-day finding of the head of Osiris two reflections of one older Egyptian ritual rule, rather than an accidental same-number match?
preregistered_discriminators: A pre-Plutarch Egyptian witness must bind an explicit day 19 to finding/recovering Osiris or an Osirian body relic.
Same numeral without recovery semantics does not pass.
Same recovery semantics in a different civil month does not establish the same calendrical event.
Older head-relic evidence without a day-19 binding supports motif ancestry but not an exact temporal rule.
Direct literary dependence requires a demonstrable transmission path, not chronological priority alone.

plutarch_inventio_osiridis.date_context: Roman Imperial period; later than the Ptolemaic Papyrus Jumilhac
plutarch_inventio_osiridis.calendar_month: Athyr/Hathor, third month of Akhet in the civil calendar
plutarch_inventio_osiridis.ritual_description: After mourning beginning on the seventeenth, priests go to the sea at night on the nineteenth, bring a sacred chest with a small golden coffer, pour in potable water, and the company raises a joyful shout that Osiris is found.

papyrus_jumilhac.date: Ptolemaic period; Louvre range 332-30 BCE; UCL summary approximately 100 BCE
papyrus_jumilhac.sequence: Day 19 head; 20 eyes; 21 jaws; 22 neck/arm; 23 innards; 24 intestines; 25 lungs/phallus; 26 thighs/legs; 27 leg/fingers; 28 phallus/arm; 29 heart; 30 arm/Horus sons plus Djed raising.
papyrus_jumilhac.scholarly_control: Sandra L. Lippert explicitly reads the head of Osiris as found on day 19 of the fourth month of Akhet (Khoiak) and the following days as collection of the other members; the 19-30 Khoiak sequence belongs to the Khoiak ritual complex.

same_semantic_family.jumilhac: the head of Osiris is found, initiating recovery of further members

pre_plutarch_priority.reason: Papyrus Jumilhac is Ptolemaic and therefore predates Plutarch's Imperial-period account.

same_civil_month.offset: one 30-day civil month apart by month/day labels

same_object_found.jumilhac: head of Osiris as a specific relic, followed by member-by-member recovery

direct_textual_dependence.reason: Chronological priority and semantic similarity do not identify Plutarch's priestly/local source or prove copying from the Jumilhac tradition.

new_kingdom_khoiak_day19.source_family: Medinet Habu / Neferhotep and comparative Khoiak evidence
new_kingdom_khoiak_day19.detail: UCL's comparative table has no Medinet Habu day-19 recovery entry; the older New Kingdom cycle clearly contains Osirian planting/mortuary rites but does not preserve the Jumilhac day-19 head-finding rule in this witness.

dendera_day19.date_context: early Roman-period Dendera Khoiak chapel comparison
dendera_day19.note: Other Dendera ritual sections can place figure-manufacture transitions around day 19, but the comparative day table does not equate Dendera day 19 with finding the head of Osiris. Dendera must therefore not be used as an independent exact head-finding duplicate of Jumilhac.

nineteenth_dynasty_abydos_head_relic.source: Seti I / Ramesses-period Abydos processional evidence assessed by Katherine J. Eaton
nineteenth_dynasty_abydos_head_relic.finding: By the Nineteenth Dynasty the Osiris Fetish appears to have represented the head reliquary of Osiris-Khentyimentiu; Ptolemaic ritual records preserve related Osirian processional/image sets.

H1_accidental_number_match.reason: The match is not numeral-only: both sources bind day 19 to an Osirian finding/recovery semantic.

H2_shared_egyptian_ritual_schema.reason: A pre-Plutarch Egyptian text already has DAY19 + FIND_OSIRIAN_RELIC, while older Abydos evidence preserves a head-reliquary motif. This supports inheritance from Egyptian ritual tradition without proving one fixed calendar rule.

H3_direct_jumilhac_to_plutarch_dependenc.reason: No transmission chain from the local Hardai/Jumilhac redaction to Plutarch's reported rite has yet been established.

H4_calendar_relocation_or_ritual_operato.definition: The semantic operator FIND_OSIRIS/FIND_RELIC may have been preserved while its civil-month placement differed among regional or historical Osirian festival programs.
H4_calendar_relocation_or_ritual_operato.critical_prediction: An intermediate Egyptian witness should preserve the day-19 finding operator in Athyr, Khoiak, or explicitly transfer/synchronize the two festival contexts.

H5_universal_day19_osiris_recovery_rule.reason: Medinet Habu, Koptos, and Dendera controls do not all assign recovery semantics to day 19.

key_upgrade_from_parent: The parent gate treated DAY_19_RECOVERY as a candidate requiring dependence testing. This successor upgrades one component: there is now a documented pre-Plutarch Egyptian DAY19 + Osirian-relic-finding witness in Papyrus Jumilhac. It does not upgrade the motif to a universal calendar law because the months and ritual objects differ and older controls do not reproduce the exact rule.
best_current_answer: A genuine bridge exists one level below a return-date claim: DAY 19 plus finding/recovering Osiris or an Osirian relic is demonstrably Egyptian and pre-Plutarch. However, the surviving witnesses do not establish one fixed ancient calendar rule: Jumilhac places the head-finding on 19 Khoiak, while Plutarch places the joyful finding of Osiris on 19 Athyr. The most productive next test is whether the FIND_OSIRIS operator migrated between regional/monthly festival calendars or derives from an older source layer not yet isolated.
